pages.x: In 1957 the Gold Coast became Ghana, the first colony south of the Sahara to win its independence. Its leader, Kwame Nkrumah, who had led strikes and been jailed by the British, told the crowds at midnight that Ghana was free for ever, and that its freedom meant nothing unless all of Africa was free.

In 1960 alone seventeen African countries became independent, most of them from France, among them Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, Madagascar and the Congo. The British prime minister Harold Macmillan told South Africa's parliament that a wind of change was blowing through the continent.

Belgium left the Congo in haste in 1960, with hardly any Congolese trained to run it. The young prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, made a fiery speech about colonial abuses in front of the Belgian king. Within weeks the army mutinied and a mineral-rich province broke away. Lumumba was overthrown, and in 1961 he was murdered with Belgian help.

France fought hard to keep Algeria, home to a million European settlers. From 1954 the National Liberation Front fought a war of bombings and ambushes, and the French army answered with torture and mass arrests. Hundreds of thousands died. In 1962 President de Gaulle let Algeria go, and almost all the settlers fled to France.

In Kenya the Mau Mau rising of the 1950s was crushed with great brutality, and tens of thousands of Kikuyu were held in camps. Yet the British let Jomo Kenyatta, whom they had jailed as its leader, out of prison, and in 1963 he became the first leader of an independent Kenya.

Portugal, a dictatorship, fought long wars to keep Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau, until its own army overthrew the government in 1974. The colonies were free by 1975. In Rhodesia a white minority held on until 1980, when the country became Zimbabwe.

Independence gave Africans their own flags and governments, and in 1963 they founded the Organisation of African Unity. But the new states inherited colonial borders, economies built to send raw goods abroad and few trained people, and many fell into coups, one-party rule and civil wars. Today Africa is the youngest continent.
pts: Portugal let go of its colonies in 1975
